summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's 2015 Penal Code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries up to seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained after independence and enhanced in the first post-independence penal code adopted in 2015. The UK Foreign Office records same-sex activity as a crime and confirms that no anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people.

Exposure is not limited to prosecution. The US State Department's 2023 reporting states that openly LGBTQI+ persons risk imprisonment and for that reason did not participate in the political process, and that societal discrimination against them continues. The same report found no public LGBTQ organisations and tight restrictions on expression of sexual orientation and gender identity, so LGBTQI+ people cannot freely assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship is compounded by heavy social stigma; in the early 2000s state-run radio and television aired programs detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality.

Foreign nationals are not shielded. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, a gay Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government called him a "dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country" and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local laws including the Penal Code's homosexuality provision. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one described as openly homosexual; Eritrea's ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the law prohibiting homosexual relations, and Italian diplomats condemned the action.

Detention and abuse accompany enforcement. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, known for housing political prisoners and journalists, where abuse, torture and beating of prisoners is commonplace. Gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military are reported to have suffered severe physical and verbal abuse and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers, on a 2002 UK refugee claimant account that is unconfirmed. The 2011 US State Department reporting records that the government labelled disloyal individuals "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles".

Criminalisation undermines health and care access: ILGA and some HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law, arguing it makes prevention programs directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an area of concern. There are no laws banning conversion therapy, and OutRight Action International found conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity are widespread due to social stigma; LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Eritrea and cannot adopt. The government has rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review appeal to legalize same-sex sexual activity as "in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people", with no major efforts to change or rescind existing laws, and in 2010 Eritrea, with other African states, rejected the Yogyakarta Principles. The UK raised these concerns bilaterally and via the EU.
tangentialFactors:
Eritrea's criminalisation sits within a broader rights environment that includes torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service, recorded in the US State Department's 2010 human rights report. Detention facilities used against people suspected of same-sex conduct are the same institutions holding political prisoners and journalists, so a charge of homosexual conduct places a visitor in a system where abuse and unlawful execution have been reported. The UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office reported that the death penalty was not used in 2013.

Restrictions on freedom of expression and state censorship of LGBTQ issues compound legal risk, since identification can precede charge. Foreign LGBTQ nationals have a documented history of removal from Eritrea on the basis of local law, which distinguishes Eritrea from jurisdictions where criminalisation applies only to residents.
localsOnly: Residents face a legal regime with no anti-discrimination protection on sexual orientation or gender identity and no legal recognition of same-sex couples, including adoption. No laws ban conversion therapy, and conversion therapy is reported to be widespread, sometimes offered in place of prosecution. Gays and lesbians in national service report abuse from superiors and fellow soldiers. Societal stigma and censorship restrict public assembly and association for LGBTQ Eritreans, and no public LGBTQ organisations exist.
outOfScopeNotes: The military abuse account rests on a single 2002 UK refugee claimant account and is unconfirmed. The current status of Article 310(1) as applied in practice, the actual frequency of prosecution, and whether the enhanced 2015 sentence has been imposed are not sourced in this inventory. No youth-specific care findings are recorded. The UK Foreign Office report carries a 2015 copyright date, so its currency relative to the 2023 US State Department reporting is unresolved.
